newsitem.title: ITALY: Troubled Alitalia has sober 50th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Alitalia has sober 50th birthday.

text.p: Debt-ridden Italian flag carrier Alitalia, battling to get a rescue plan off the ground, celebrated its 50th birthday soberly on Monday saying a big party would be inappropriate given its strained circumstances.
Air traffic controllers further dampened the festivities by staging a four-hour strike which caused severe delays.
But managing director Domenico Cempella was upbeat, saying Alitalia was looking to the future with confidence.
"We are determined to get over our troubles and we are succeeding," he told Italian state television RAI.
He sent a message to staff marking the 50th anniversary, saying he was certain that "it was a wise decision to avoid big festivities which could look inopportune to our customers".

They faced hours of delays and disruption as a result of the air traffic controllers' strike. More than 100 of a total 735 arrivals or departures at Rome's Fiumicino airport were cancelled and many of Alitalia's own flights were affected.

Nevertheless, the airline welcomed passengers on a special flight from Turin to Rome with a birthday message as Alitalia symbolically re-traced its maiden flight on May 5, 1947. At that time Alitalia was 40 percent owned by British European Airways and 40 percent by state holding IRI, and counted a civilian version of the World War Two Lancaster bomber among its fleet. Private investors held 20 percent.

Today, after carrying 350 million passengers some 4.5 billion km (2.8 billion miles), Alitalia is struggling to emerge from nine consecutive years in the red via a recapitalisation programme and sees eventual privatisation on the horizon.

"We're striving to balance our books in 1997," Cempella told RAI, adding that with the restructuring and a major revamp of Milan's Malpensa airport in place by 1998, the airline would be looking for a strategic international alliance.
Such a link-up was "unavoidable for a company like Alitalia", Cempella said. He gave no other details.
The first hurdle, however, remains the company's restructuring plan, which the European Union's executive Commission last month sent back to the Italian government for changes.

Italy last year requested EU permission for a capital injection worth more than three trillion lire ($1.7 billion). The government has already authorised IRI, which now owns some 90 percent of Alitalia, to hand over 1.5 trillion lire.
Cempella accused Brussels of prejudice after Alitalia had already agreed to alter some proposals, including reducing the overall size of the capital increase to 2.8 trillion lire.
The Commission gave no details of the changes it had suggested in a letter sent to the Italian government.
Alitalia ended months of bitter conflict with unions in June last year when it sealed a landmark deal to slash hefty personnel costs and boost productivity.

As part of the rescue plan, cabin crew and ground staff agreed to a deal which would give them up to 30 percent of the company and three seats on the board in return for 2,000 job cuts from a work force of 17,000.
Cempella has called the radical plan, which will run in two phases until the year 2000, "the only way" to avoid bankruptcy. ($1=1,711 lire)
